name: Jericho
info: Jericho is a city in the Jordan Valley of the West Bank, beside a spring, where archaeologists have found more than 20 successive settlements, the first dating to about 9500 BCE, and where the Hebrew Bible places a siege led by Joshua.

facts.founded: The first permanent settlement developed near the Ein es-Sultan spring between 9,500 and 9000 BCE, after Natufian hunter-gatherers had camped there from about 10,000 BCE.
facts.where: In an oasis in the Jordan Valley, 258 m below sea level, with the Jordan River to the east and Jerusalem to the west, in the West Bank.
facts.known: Remains of more than 20 successive settlements; a Neolithic wall and tower; plastered skulls; Middle Bronze Age fortifications; the Hebrew Bible's account of Joshua; Hasmonean and Herodian winter palaces; the Gospels; Byzantine synagogues; Hisham's Palace
facts.today: Jericho is a city in the West Bank, the capital of the Jericho Governorate, under Palestinian Authority administration since 1994.

t: Jericho grew from a Natufian camping ground beside a spring into a settlement with a stone wall and tower, and later into a fortified Canaanite city that reached its greatest Bronze Age extent between 1700 and 1550 BCE.

The ancient city was destroyed in the Late Bronze Age or soon after and was occupied again from the 11th century BCE, and in the Hasmonean and Herodian periods a new Jericho of palaces and gardens was built on both banks of Wadi Qelt.

In the Byzantine period the town moved about 1,600 metres east to the site on which the modern town is centred, and it passed in turn to Muslim, Crusader, Ayyubid, Ottoman, British, Jordanian and Israeli rule.
dyk: A hundred men would have needed more than a hundred days to build the Neolithic wall and tower of Jericho, which suggests some kind of social organisation; the tower stood over 8.5 metres high and held an internal staircase of 22 stone steps.
ev: The first permanent settlement develops near the Ein es-Sultan spring
A stone wall and tower are built at Tell es-Sultan during the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A
The Early Bronze Age settlement reaches its largest extent
The Middle Bronze Age city is destroyed
Herod begins to rule Judea and later greatly expands the royal domain at Jericho
A Christian pilgrim describes Jericho, and soon afterwards the Byzantine town is built to the east
The Ayyubid forces of Saladin evict the Crusaders
Administrative control of Jericho passes to the Palestinian Authority

sections.origins:
Jericho lies in the Jordan Valley, with the Jordan River to the east and Jerusalem to the west, 258 metres below sea level in an oasis in Wadi Qelt. The spring of Ein es-Sultan produces 3.8 cubic metres of water per minute and irrigates some 10 square kilometres, and copious springs in and around the city have attracted settlement for thousands of years. The Biblical Hebrew name Yəriḥo is generally thought to derive from the Canaanite word rēḥ, 'fragrant', though other theories derive it from the Canaanite word Yaraḥ, 'moon', or from the lunar deity Yarikh, for whom the city was an early centre of worship.

The earliest excavated settlement stood at Tell es-Sultan, a couple of kilometres from the current city. Evidence of settlement goes back to about 10,000 BCE, when Natufian hunter-gatherers camped by the spring during the cold and drought of the Younger Dryas and left crescent-shaped microliths. Around 9600 BCE the drought and cold ended, and the groups stayed longer, eventually living there all year. The first permanent settlement developed near the spring between 9,500 and 9000 BCE, in the culture archaeologists call Pre-Pottery Neolithic A. Its houses were circular, about 5 metres across, built of sun-dried clay and straw bricks, and the dead were buried under the floors. Its people domesticated emmer wheat, barley and pulses and hunted wild animals.
sections.growth:
At Tell es-Sultan the Pre-Pottery Neolithic settlement covered 40,000 square metres and was surrounded by a stone wall over 3.6 metres high and 1.8 metres wide at the base, with a stone tower over 8.5 metres high inside it. Carbon dates indicate that the tower was built around 8300 BCE and used until about 7800 BCE. The wall may have served as a defence against flood water, and the tower may have been used for ceremonies. Estimates of the population range from 200 to 300 up to 2,000 to 3,000, and the town had round mud-brick houses but no street planning. After a hiatus of around five centuries a second settlement was founded in 6800 BCE, with rectilinear mud-brick buildings and ten plastered human skulls painted to reconstruct the faces of individuals.

A succession of settlements followed from 4500 BCE. In the Early Bronze Age Jericho became a fortified town, and around 2600 BCE the settlement reached its largest extent. In the Middle Bronze Age it was a small prominent city of Canaan, with extensive defensive walls strengthened by rectangular towers, and it reached its greatest Bronze Age extent between 1700 and 1550 BCE. Kathleen Kenyon thought the Middle Bronze Age perhaps the most prosperous in the whole history of Canaan. Its cemetery held shaft-tombs with elaborate offerings, which may reflect the emergence of local kings.
sections.rulers:
After the Middle Bronze Age city fell, Jericho recovered on a smaller scale in the Late Bronze Age, between 1450 and 1200 BCE. A structure known as the Middle Building apparently housed the city's local rulers, then vassals of the Egyptian empire. Occupation resumed at Tell es-Sultan in the 11th century BCE, and the town was fortified in the 10th century. In the Persian period Jericho was an administrative centre of Yehud Medinata, the province of Judah, and between 336 and 323 BCE it served as the private estate of Alexander the Great. In the middle of the 2nd century BCE it was under Seleucid rule, and in the second half of that century it became part of the kingdom of Judea under the Hasmoneans.

In 63 BCE Pompey passed through on his way to besiege Jerusalem, and Judaea came under Roman oversight. Herod began to rule Judea in 37 BCE; he first leased the royal estate at Jericho from Cleopatra, and after 30 BCE Octavian gave him full control of it. Herod's son Herod Archelaus rebuilt the palace after unrest following Herod's death. Jericho became a small Roman garrison settlement by around 100 CE. In the Byzantine period it became a Christian town. Jericho later formed part of Jund Filastin in the Umayyad period, followed by the Abbasid and Fatimid dynasties, and was held by the Crusaders until 1187. Ottoman rule began in 1517 and was followed by British rule, Jordanian rule from 1948, Israeli occupation from 1967 and Palestinian Authority administration from 1994.
sections.life:
The Hasmoneans built royal winter palaces at Tulul Abu el-'Alayiq and laid out a garden city around them on both banks of Wadi Qelt. Aqueducts supplied the palaces and a farming and workshop complex that cultivated balsam and persimmon and produced date wine. Jericho served as an agricultural centre, a crossroads and a winter resort for Jerusalem's aristocracy. Josephus called its district the most fruitful country of Judea, rich in date palms and balsam, and Strabo described the plain, the Palace and the Balsam Park. A large Jewish cemetery of the 1st century CE has a rock-cut tomb with painted decoration and 22 ossuaries inscribed in Greek, Hebrew and Aramaic. The Christian Gospels state that Jesus passed through Jericho, where he healed blind beggars and met the chief tax collector Zacchaeus, and the road from Jerusalem to Jericho is the setting of the Parable of the Good Samaritan.

In the Byzantine period many monasteries and churches were built, among them the Monastery of Saint George of Choziba in 340 CE, and at least two synagogues were built in the 6th century. The Jericho synagogue had a mosaic inscribed 'Peace upon Israel'. Under Islamic rule irrigated agriculture was developed, and al-Maqdisi wrote in 985 that the water of Jericho was held to be the best in all Islam. The Crusaders raised sugar production to a large-scale industry. In 1596 the Ottoman tax registers listed 51 households, all Muslim.
sections.crises:
The Hebrew Bible tells of the Battle of Jericho, led by Joshua, in which the Canaanite city fell as the first city captured by the Israelites in the Promised Land. The historicity of the biblical account is not generally accepted by scholars. Lorenzo Nigro suggests that the story may have developed from local memories of destructions the Canaanite city suffered in the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE, which the biblical writers later used. Archaeologically, the Middle Bronze Age city fell in the 16th century BCE, and carbon from its destruction layer dates to 1617 to 1530 BCE. The Iron Age town was destroyed in the Babylonian conquest of Judah in the late 6th century BCE.

Around 135 or 134 BCE the Hasmonean leader Simon Thassi was assassinated by his son-in-law Ptolemy, the strategos of Jericho, at the nearby fortress of Duq. Herod ordered the drowning of the young high priest Aristobulus III in a pool of the Jericho palace. After Herod's death the palace was plundered and set on fire. During the First Jewish Revolt the inhabitants had fled into the hills before the Romans arrived in 68 CE, and after Jerusalem fell in 70 Jericho declined quickly. The monasteries were abandoned after the Sasanian invasion of 614. An earthquake destroyed Jericho in 659, and the pilgrim Arculf found it in ruins a decade later. An earthquake in 747 largely destroyed the unfinished palace at Khirbet al-Mafjar. After the Crusaders were evicted in 1187 the town slowly went into decline, and in 1659 the French traveller d'Arvieux called it desolate, with about fifty poor houses. A quake in 1927 killed around 300 people.
sections.legacy:
Jericho is described in the Bible as the 'city of palm trees', and Josephus, Strabo, Diodorus Siculus and Pliny the Elder all wrote of its palms and balsam. Excavations began in 1868 with Charles Warren and continued with Sellin and Watzinger, John Garstang, Kathleen Kenyon between 1952 and 1958, and an Italian-Palestinian project from 1997. Jericho is the type site of the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A and B periods. In 2023 Tell es-Sultan, also called Old Jericho, was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in the State of Palestine and described as the 'oldest fortified city in the world'. Other remains include the Hasmonean and Herodian palaces, the Byzantine synagogues, Hisham's Palace at Khirbet al-Mafjar and the Crusader sugar mills of Tawahin es-Sukkar.

The city today is in the West Bank, Palestine, and is the capital of the Jericho Governorate. Israel has occupied the West Bank since the Six-Day War of 1967, and Jericho was the first city handed to Palestinian Authority control under the Oslo Accords, by the Gaza–Jericho Agreement of 4 May 1994. It lies in an enclave in Area A, surrounded by land in Area C under Israeli military control. It had a population of 20,907 in 2017.

summary: Jericho, in the Jordan Valley of the West Bank, grew around a spring from a settlement of about 9500 BCE with a Neolithic wall and tower into a Canaanite city, and later a Hasmonean and Herodian garden city. The Hebrew Bible tells of its fall to Joshua. Tell es-Sultan was inscribed by UNESCO in 2023.
references: Jerome Murphy-O'Connor, The Holy Land: An Oxford Archaeological Guide from Earliest Times to 1700 (Oxford University Press, 1998)
Lorenzo Nigro, Gerico: La città millenaria (Hoepli Editore, 2025)

The article gives the Middle Bronze destruction layer as 1617-1530 BCE (carbon) and c. 1573; I wrote only the range and '16th century'. Its statement that the city was 'destroyed in the Late Bronze Age, after which it no longer served as an urban centre' contradicts its later text on a recovered Late Bronze Age city and an Iron Age town; I left that sentence out.

Biblical account: stated as what the Hebrew Bible tells, with the article's remarks on historicity and Nigro's suggestion. The article gives no archaeological dating of a Joshua-era destruction other than the Middle Bronze layer and scarcity of 13th-century material; I did not link them.
'Wall and tower built around 8000 BCE' (article) vs carbon dates 8300 BCE: I used the carbon dates in the text and 'c. 8000 BCE' in the event, as the article states both. Editor may harmonise.

Chronology list in BC (Nigro 2016) left out. Article's PPNB dates (7220-5850 BCE) and the second settlement 6800 BCE are inconsistent with 'five-century hiatus'; I used only the 6800 BCE settlement and hiatus.

Present status: the article says occupied by Israel since 1967 and that Jericho is in Palestine; no dispute over the city's status is stated beyond that, so I gave the article's facts and attributed nothing further. Editor to check that this fits the brief's 'each side's position attributed'.
